rv.q: Above all, it’s laugh-out-loud funny.
And what is never in doubt is the sizzle of the songs by Robert Lopez (Frozen) and Jeff Marx, and the brilliance of the puppeteers in Jason Moore’s effervescent staging.

Every number is performed with such physical and vocal exuberance by the cast of actor-puppeteers, especially the spectacular Harrison and Benjamin, that it really does seem as if the puppets are doing the talking, singing and shagging.
Avenue Q’s bawdy puppets are back – and more outrageous than ever

The superb young cast, led by Noah Harrison and Emily Benjamin, manipulate a collection of hand-held puppets, designed by Rick Lyon, that are brought to life with the simplest of gestures and interact with humans including Amelia Kinu Muus’s terminally dissatisfied Asian-American wife. The American Dream hasn’t quite delivered the goods
The profane puppet musical back in town, and if it no longer feels audacious, it is very charming
At the end of the day, Avenue Q is a hilarious hoot, and I have no hesitation in recommending this delightful and hearty production.
The greatest triumph of this fantastically entertaining show is how its message is as forthright now as it was then, and needed more than ever.

As filthy, funny and gloriously sharp as ever, this revival understands exactly why the show endures, and with a limited run here at the Shaftesbury, forget Sesame Street, you need to be asking how to get to Avenue Q.
Rude, crude and totally unsuitable for children; it's great to have it back.
I couldn’t have loved this special production of Avenue Q any more if I tried.
None of this ultimately undermines a comically pristine show which puts the 'heart', and indeed the 'felt', in 'heartfelt'.
Almost exactly 20 years after Avenue Q first came to the West End, it’s back, and it’s as brilliant as ever.
The show suddenly becomes as fresh as ever.
Avenue Q at the Shaftesbury Theatre is uproariously funny, unexpectedly moving and brilliantly re-energised for the present day.
Growing up is still as hard as ever and Avenue Q has never made that point so perfectly.
Nevertheless this is a masterly cast, who play a trifecta of roles as controller of the puppets, the voices of the puppet characters and then the real human characters.
It’s full of energy, laugh-out-loud moments, and hasn’t lost an ounce of its iconic chaos along the way.
There's an uplifting message of community, acceptance, and the compromises of adulthood.
Their laughter and engagement suggest the show successfully taps into both nostalgia and present-day relevance.

cn.t: The profane puppet musical remains fresh and funny 20 years later, with critics praising its clever songs, irreverent humor, and energetic cast, though some note its shock value has diminished since 2006.
